Jeddah airport cancelled 156 flights, constituting 20 percent of all scheduled flights, while 374 flights, or 49 percent, were delayed. Saturday’s attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed 12 people and injured 309, according to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation. The death toll subsequently rose to 13 after an Indian national who had been injured in the strike died, according to Reuters. A separate attack on Sunday killed a Pakistani resident and injured 11 others, according to the Saudi authorities. Airlines have also suspended services to the Saudi capital. When Aoun was elected president in January 2025, Hezbollah supported his election, helping end a prolonged presidential vacancy. But the political understanding that facilitated his election did not resolve the fundamental disagreement over Hezbollah’s independent military structure and the state’s authority to decide matters of war and peace. From the beginning of his presidency, Aoun made clear that he wanted weapons brought under state control. In his inaugural address, he pledged to affirm the state’s right to monopolise arms, linking the principle to strengthening the Lebanese Armed Forces, protecting the country’s borders and implementing international resolutions. His position became more explicit in a speech marking Army Day in July 2025, when he called for the army and security forces to have the exclusive right to bear arms, urging Hezbollah and its supporters to “place your bet solely on the Lebanese state”. north.title: Can Turkey and Pakistan defend Saudi Arabia from the Houthis?
north.text: Turkey and Pakistan's promise of rapid military support for Saudi Arabia faces a more urgent test after weekend attacks on Riyadh’s international airport killed 12 people and forced its closure. Turning that commitment into effective protection will depend on what its partners can spare, how their forces operate alongside Saudi units and how far Ankara and Islamabad are willing to enter the conflict . At an emergency meeting in Riyadh on 5 October, the three countries pledged to implement their collective defence commitments and rapidly deploy agreed forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia, subject to their national legislation. The decision marked a significant step for the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement they signed in August, but left troop numbers, equipment, missions, and deployment schedules publicly unspecified. Their contributions also begin from different positions. Pakistan already has an established military presence in the kingdom and has reportedly supplied weapons and advisers to Yemeni government forces. Turkey is considering additional defensive assistance while explicitly ruling out offensive operations abroad under the pact. The immediate test is whether these commitments can address Saudi vulnerabilities quickly enough to matter - and whether protecting the kingdom can remain separate from supporting its campaign in Yemen. What Riyadh needs Saudi Arabia’s requirement extends beyond additional troops. In September, drones struck the East-West Pipeline south of Medina , causing injuries and damage and prompting a precautionary shutdown of the route carrying crude to Red Sea export terminals. ukraine.title: Replacing equipment at Yandex data centers damaged by Ukrainian drone strikes will take about six months, Kommersant reports
ukraine.text: Replacing the equipment destroyed in Ukrainian strikes on Yandex’s data centers could take up to six months, sources in the IT market told the Russian business daily Kommersant. Yandex will likely begin buying equipment through various channels, including foreign ones, to replace what was lost more quickly, the outlet’s sources said. Prices for “hardware” are expected to rise in the short term, and Yandex will have to buy equipment “on the most expensive market in recent years,” the sources said. “These were very large data centers, and since they were built, a global shortage and price increase for computing power, especially AI accelerators, has begun. Equipping them is going to be expensive and lengthy,” Sergei Kudryashov of Strategy Partners told the outlet. The additional costs will ultimately lead to higher prices for cloud services for customers, the outlet’s sources said. Ukrainian drones have struck three of Yandex’s six known data centers over the past several days. Users in Russia and abroad have faced outages in Yandex’s services, including its taxi service. Yandex itself restricted downloads from its Yandex Disk cloud storage service in order to “maintain the operability” of its other services after the attack on the data centers. ukraine.title: Ukrainian defence tech company Phantom Defense acquires anti-drone net developer, unveils counter-UAV system – photos, videos
ukraine.text: Ukrainian defence tech company Phantom Defense has acquired Karakurt, which develops nets designed to ensnare drones, bringing its team on board. The company has also unveiled its new Manhal counter-UAV system. Source: Phantom Defense in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda Details: Phantom Defense has signed an agreement to acquire Karakurt in full and integrate its technologies into its own ecosystem. "The integration of net-based UAV interception technologies into the Phantom Defense ecosystem will enhance protection for frontline units and infrastructure against a range of unmanned threats," the company noted. A Karakurt drone net on a DJI Mavic 3 drone Photo: Phantom Defense The Karakurt system uses a special launcher module to fire a net on an incoming drone. The net tangles around its propellers, preventing them from spinning freely and bringing the drone down. Phantom Defense says Karakurt's nets can bring down enemy drones without blowing them up, leaving the aircraft intact for Ukrainian defence forces to examine or potentially put to use. According to the company, drone nets are also cheaper to produce and maintain than anti-aircraft missile and artillery systems, allowing them to be deployed widely among units along the line of contact. A DJI Mavic 3 drone equipped with a Karakurt anti-drone net Photo: Phantom Defense The use of drone nets also helps minimise the risk of collateral damage caused by explosions and debris. The company says this makes the technology suitable for defending critical infrastructure and civilian facilities against various drone threats. Karakurt systems come in several variants, tailored to different drone types and operating conditions. The M3, M4 and A4 models, compatible with DJI Mavic, Matrice and Autel platforms, fire nets downwards

yemen.title: Can Turkey and Pakistan defend Saudi Arabia from the Houthis?
yemen.text: Turkey and Pakistan's promise of rapid military support for Saudi Arabia faces a more urgent test after weekend attacks on Riyadh’s international airport killed 12 people and forced its closure. Turning that commitment into effective protection will depend on what its partners can spare, how their forces operate alongside Saudi units and how far Ankara and Islamabad are willing to enter the conflict . At an emergency meeting in Riyadh on 5 October, the three countries pledged to implement their collective defence commitments and rapidly deploy agreed forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia, subject to their national legislation. The decision marked a significant step for the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement they signed in August, but left troop numbers, equipment, missions, and deployment schedules publicly unspecified. Their contributions also begin from different positions. Pakistan already has an established military presence in the kingdom and has reportedly supplied weapons and advisers to Yemeni government forces. Turkey is considering additional defensive assistance while explicitly ruling out offensive operations abroad under the pact. The immediate test is whether these commitments can address Saudi vulnerabilities quickly enough to matter - and whether protecting the kingdom can remain separate from supporting its campaign in Yemen. What Riyadh needs Saudi Arabia’s requirement extends beyond additional troops. In September, drones struck the East-West Pipeline south of Medina , causing injuries and damage and prompting a precautionary shutdown of the route carrying crude to Red Sea export terminals. Submitted by MEE staff on Mon, 10/12/2026 - 09:45 Yemen's war has reignited, pulling in Saudi Arabia's allies and threatening one of the world's most important shipping lanes Supporters of Ansar Allah hold up a portrait of the group's leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, during a protest against the Saudi intervention in Yemen in Sanaa on 18 September 2026 (AFP) Off A strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday killed 13 people and wounded 309, in the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in more than a decade. Another strike on the airport on Sunday killed one more person. The Saudi -led coalition blamed Yemen 's Houthis and called the attack a war crime. In a statement on Sunday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had targeted the airport "in three stages" since Friday evening, closing it completely, and warned that Saudi airports were "unsafe", except those serving Mecca and Medina. The attack capped a summer of escalation. A UN-backed truce that had largely frozen Yemen's war since 2022 broke down in July after Saudi Arabia bombed Sanaa airport, and the Houthis then declared a maritime blockade on the kingdom. In September, the Sanaa-based group seized the Red Sea port of Mokha and pushed towards the Bab al-Mandab strait . Saudi-backed government forces launched a counter-offensive in early October, and the UN special envoy has warned that Yemen has returned to full-scale war . Heavy clashes are continuing around the strategically important city of Taiz, which sits above the Red Sea coast. The renewed fighting has displaced 130,000 people . Who are the Houthis? yemen.title: Which airlines have cancelled Saudi flights amid Houthi attacks?
yemen.text: Major international airlines have suspended flights to Saudi Arabia following escalating Houthi attacks and threats against airports across the kingdom, leaving passengers facing cancellations, delays and diversions. The disruption follows a series of attacks on Riyadh's main airport over the weekend that killed at least 12 people and injured more than 300, forcing authorities to temporarily close King Khalid International Airport. The Houthis have warned that Saudi airports remain potential targets, raising concerns about further disruption to international air travel. Some airlines have suspended services until mid-October, while others have extended cancellations until the end of the month. Here's what to know about the flight cancellations, affected airports and travel warnings. Which airlines have suspended flights to Saudi Arabia? Several major international airlines have suspended flights to Riyadh, while others have cancelled selected services to Jeddah and Dammam. According to Reuters , Lufthansa Group has suspended flights to Riyadh until 16 October, while Air France-KLM has halted services to the Saudi capital until the end of the month. Other airlines have announced the following cancellations: Flydubai: All flights to and from Riyadh cancelled through 14 October. Air India: Riyadh services suspended until 15 October. Air India Express: Riyadh flights suspended until 14 October. SriLankan Airlines: Riyadh services suspended until 18 October. Etihad Airways: Selected flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam cancelled between 11 and 13 October. Emirates: Flights between Dubai and Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam affected by cancellations on Monday, 12 October. Air Arabia: Cancellations and schedule changes affecting Saudi routes. yemen.title: UK advises against using any Saudi airport except Medina
yemen.text: UK advises against using any Saudi airport except Medina Submitted by Imran Mulla on Mon, 10/12/2026 - 09:12 The UK has further warned British nationals not to try and leave Saudi Arabia via airports in the country An air traffic control tower is seen at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on 19 September 2026 (AFP) Off The British government has advised its citizens against all but essential travel to parts of Saudi Arabia , including Jeddah and Dammam, and to all airports in the country except Medina International Airport. The UK has further warned British nationals not to try and leave Saudi Arabia via airports in the country. This comes after a fresh attack on a passenger terminal at Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, which killed at least one person and wounded 11. Saturday's attack on the airport killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300 - making it the deadliest strike on a Gulf country since the US-Israeli war on Iran began on 28 February. Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement that four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis , one American , one Egyptian , one Jordanian , one Syrian , one Palestinian and one Sudanese were killed in the attack. It was the third attack on the airport in a week, following earlier strikes that killed four people and damaged a Saudi commercial aircraft. The British Foreign Office updated its official guidance on Sunday to advise UK nationals against "all but essential travel to all airports within Saudi Arabia except for Medina International Airport", as well as "all but essential travel to Aseer province, Riyadh province, Najran province, Jizan province and the cities of Taif, Jeddah and Dammam". yemen.title: Alvarez vs M'billi fight will go ahead in Riyadh despite attacks
yemen.text: Saul "Canelo" Alvarez will fight in his world title bout against Christian M'billi in Saudi Arabia this month, promoter Turki Al-Sheikh said after a strike on Riyadh's international airport killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement claimed responsibility for Saturday's attack, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. On Sunday, one more person was killed and nearly a dozen hurt in another attack on the international airport in Riyadh, where Alvarez and WBC super-middleweight champion M'billi are set to clash on 31 October. "Canelo reached out and told me he'll still fight in Riyadh this October, no matter what happens. He fears nothing," said Al-Sheikh, chairman of Saudi Arabia 's General Entertainment Authority, in a post on social media on Sunday. Alvarez's representatives did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside business hours in Mexico. The Mexican boxer, a former two-time undisputed super-middleweight champion, has not fought since he was beaten by American Terence Crawford in September 2025.
